chapterTitle: Classes, Objects, and Basic Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Concepts
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute mixed media lesson. Begin with a conceptual animation explaining classes as blueprints and objects as instances, using a `Car` analogy (Car class, red car object, blue car object). Transition to live coding: create a new C# class `PlayerStats` (NOT `MonoBehaviour`) with `public string playerName`, `private int health`, a constructor, and `public void TakeDamage(int amount)`. Then, create a `PlayerController` (a `MonoBehaviour`) that instantiates `PlayerStats` objects (`PlayerStats player1 = new PlayerStats(...)`). Show how to access public fields and call methods. Highlight the `private` health field and demonstrate attempting to access it directly (showing a compile error), then show using a public method to modify it (`TakeDamage`). Conclude by explicitly comparing the roles of `PlayerStats` (data model) and `PlayerController` (Unity component) with a clear diagram. Include a mini-quiz on identifying classes vs. objects.

---

screens.title: Classes, Objects, and Basic OOP
screens.narratorSegment: Today you will learn how object-oriented design helps structure game code by separating data models from Unity components. Imagine a car template that describes color, speed, and a drive action. That template is a class. When you build a red car and a blue car from that template, those are objects, each holding their own state but sharing behaviors. In Unity you often use a lightweight data class for the model and a MonoBehaviour for the scene behavior. This separation makes systems easier to test, reuse, and reason about. As we go, you'll see concrete C# examples: a PlayerStats data class with a private health field and a public TakeDamage method, and a PlayerController MonoBehaviour that instantiates PlayerStats and calls its methods. You will also learn why constructors matter, how the new keyword creates instances, and how public and private control who can read or modify data. By the end you'll be able to design a simple Enemy or Inventory item class and connect it to a MonoBehaviour manager. Consider now: which parts of your game are pure data models and which belong on GameObjects?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: A class is a blueprint; an object is its concrete instance. Use custom classes for data models and MonoBehaviour for scene behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Classes & Objects
Car analogy: class vs object
A class describes parts and behaviors; objects are each physical car made from that template.
Class (blueprint)
Defines color, maxSpeed, Drive method. No position or runtime ties.
Object (instance)
Red car with fuel 80 and current speed 0. Separate state from other cars.
Why this matters
Organizing code into classes and instances keeps data local, avoids global state, and lets you reuse behavior across many objects.
In this lesson
Code-first walkthrough: create data classes and manage them from a MonoBehaviour
You will build a PlayerStats data model and a PlayerController that instantiates it, showing constructors, fields, methods, and encapsulation in practice.
Explore Key Topics
Blueprints
Define data and behavior for objects.
Instances
Create objects with their own state using new.
Encapsulation
Use access modifiers to protect internal state.
Live-coding preview
PlayerStats and PlayerController pattern. Code shown for study and practice.
// PlayerStats.cs - custom class (not a MonoBehaviour)
public class PlayerStats {
    public string playerName;
    private int health;
    public PlayerStats(string name, int hp) { /* initialize state */ }
    public void TakeDamage(int amount) { /* reduce health safely */ }
}
Runtime flow
  • 1. MonoBehaviour creates PlayerStats with new.
  • 2. MonoBehaviour calls public methods to change state.
  • 3. Private fields remain protected from external change.
Key Takeaway: Keep data models separate for easier testing and reuse.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain classes, objects, and encapsulation in your own words, define a custom C# class and its constructor, create object instances and interact with their fields and methods, and relate these custom classes to Unity MonoBehaviour components. First, you will learn to identify where data belongs: in a reusable class or attached to a scene object. Second, you will write a constructor that safely initializes an object's state and see why constructors prevent uninitialized data. Third, you will practice creating instances using the new keyword and calling public methods to change state rather than mutating private fields directly. Finally, you will map these ideas to Unity: when to use a MonoBehaviour to run scene logic and when to use a plain class as a data model. Each objective links a practical skill to why it matters in game code, and you'll complete a small hands-on activity creating inventory items and a manager to hold them. These skills reduce bugs and make your systems easier to extend.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Activity
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide ties skills to a hands-on activity. You will create an InventoryItem class as a pure data model and then manage instances from an InventoryManager MonoBehaviour. That practice teaches how to store multiple objects in a List and iterate over them. You will see how constructors initialize each item's properties and how private fields are protected from outside mutation, while public methods allow controlled changes like using a consumable. The activity reinforces why we separate visual, scene-managed behavior from plain C# objects: many game systems need data only, not a full component lifecycle. During the activity you will attach the manager to a GameObject, run the scene, and observe console logs that show creation, state changes, and method calls. This exercise prepares you for typical patterns like enemy stats stored separately from enemy controllers, and it trains you to avoid direct field mutation which often causes bugs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Learning Objectives
Hands-on activity
Create InventoryItem as a non-MonoBehaviour C# class. Instantiate several items in InventoryManager. Use List to store them and call methods to use consumables.
What you will see
  • Console logs showing item creation and use.
  • Items in the list with different stack sizes.
  • Attempted direct access to a private field causes a compile error—then fix by using a public method.
Why this activity
It teaches safe state management, constructors, and how MonoBehaviour acts as the bridge to the Unity runtime.
Mini mnemonic
Think: Class = recipe, Object = baked item. The recipe belongs in code; the baked item exists at runtime.

screens.title: What is a Class? A Blueprint for Behavior and Data
screens.narratorSegment: A class is a blueprint that groups related data and behavior into a single, named unit. In game development we use classes to represent players, enemies, items, or systems. A class declares fields—variables that hold data like health or name—and methods—functions that act on that data like TakeDamage or UseItem. Defining a class lets you express a concept once and reuse that definition to create many instances. For a concrete example, the EnemyStats class defines enemyName, health, attackPower, and a TakeDamage method. The constructor sets initial values when you create an enemy. It matters because when you change the behavior in one place, all instances reflect that change. A common misconception is to think classes hold runtime-only scene references; they can be pure data models with no knowledge of Unity's lifecycle. Use small, focused classes to model data and keep Unity-specific behavior in MonoBehaviour scripts. Practice by writing a class for a collectible item with fields for name, description, id, and stack size. Then add a UseItem method that decrements stack size if the item is consumable. This teaches cohesion and simplifies testing. How would you change one method to affect all items at once?

keyIdea.title: Definition focus
keyIdea.text: A class groups data and behavior into a reusable blueprint you can instantiate many times.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › What is a Class?
Class structure
Fields hold data. Methods hold behavior. Constructors initialize an instance's starting state.
Example: InventoryItem
public class InventoryItem { public string itemName; public int stackSize; private bool isConsumable; public InventoryItem(string name, int stack, bool consumable) { /*...*/ } public void UseItem() { /*...*/ } }
Concrete exercise
Write a class for a quest or item. Make fields public for read access, and keep internal counters private.
Key Takeaway

Design classes for one responsibility: data models should not manage scene lifecycle.

Common misconception
Students sometimes attach all data to MonoBehaviour hoping Unity will serialize it. Use plain C# classes when you need lightweight models and control over construction.
Annotated example
EnemyStats defines state and behavior but has no Awake or Update. It logs creation through Unity's debug when convenient, but remains a plain data object.
Try this prompt
Sketch a class called PlayerStats. What fields does it need, and which should be private? Write a constructor signature that sets them.

screens.title: Constructors and Initializing Objects
screens.narratorSegment: Constructors are special methods that run when you create an object. They have the same name as the class and no return value. Their job is to set fields to sensible starting values so the object is ready to use. For example, in EnemyStats the constructor accepts name, initialHealth, attackPower, and isBossEnemy and assigns them to fields. When you call new EnemyStats with those arguments, the constructor runs and logs creation. Constructors prevent mistakes like uninitialized fields and let you enforce invariants—such as ensuring current health never exceeds max health. A common mistake is exposing uninitialized public fields and then forgetting to set them before use. Another misuse is putting heavy Unity-only initialization into constructors of objects that will be serialized or created differently. In Unity, prefer constructors for pure C# classes and reserve Awake or Start for MonoBehaviour lifecycle initialization. Practice: write a PlayerStats constructor that sets playerName and health, then create two instances with different starting health. How does changing the constructor signature affect existing instantiation sites? Constructors and Initializing Objects means use constructors to create valid objects and prevent uninitialized or inconsistent state.. In practical terms, how constructors set an object's starting state and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use constructors to create valid objects and prevent uninitialized or inconsistent state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Constructors
Constructor pattern
A constructor gives each object a valid initial state and documents required data.
// EnemyStats constructor (visual example)
public EnemyStats(string name, int initialHealth, float power, bool isBossEnemy) {
    enemyName = name;
    health = initialHealth;
    attackPower = power;
    _isBoss = isBossEnemy;
    Debug.Log("New enemy created: " + enemyName);
}
Key Takeaway

Constructors simplify creating valid objects and reduce runtime errors from missing initialization.

Practical notes
  • Prefer constructors for non-MonoBehaviour classes that need immediate, consistent state.
  • For MonoBehaviour, Unity calls Awake and Start; avoid using new to create MonoBehaviours.
  • Changing constructor parameters may require updating all instantiation sites—use defaults when appropriate.
Common mistake
Relying on default field values that leave an object in an invalid state when used before initialization.

screens.title: Creating Objects with new and Using Instances
screens.narratorSegment: Creating an object in C# uses the new keyword. That call allocates an instance, runs its constructor, and returns a reference you can store. In Unity, you often do this inside a MonoBehaviour method such as Awake or Start. For example, in GameManager or InventoryManager you might write new InventoryItem to create potions and swords and then add them to a List. After creating instances, you access public fields and call methods on them to change state. Importantly, each variable that holds the reference points to a distinct object; modifying one object does not change others. A typical flow is: define class, call new with constructor arguments, store the reference in a collection, and invoke methods like UseItem. A common misunderstanding is treating new as cloning; it always creates a fresh object. Another subtle point is reference semantics: when you pass an object reference to another variable or method, both refer to the same instance. Practice by instantiating two PlayerStats objects with different names and health, then call TakeDamage on one and observe that the other remains unchanged. Why does that separation help when building many enemies or items?

keyIdea.title: Instantiation flow
keyIdea.text: Use new to create distinct instances, store references in collections, and call methods to modify each object's own state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Creating Objects
Step-by-step
  1. Define the class with fields, constructor, methods.
  2. Instantiate with new and pass constructor arguments.
  3. Store references in variables or collections like List.
  4. Invoke methods to change the instance's state safely.
// InventoryManager.Start example (conceptual)
InventoryItem potion = new InventoryItem("Health Potion", "Restores health", 101, 3, true);
playerInventory.Add(potion);
potion.UseItem();
Example card
Create goblin and ogre as EnemyStats instances. Call TakeDamage on goblin. Observe goblin health change but ogre remains unchanged.
Common pitfall
Passing object references around without understanding that they point to the same instance can cause unexpected shared state changes.

screens.title: Public vs Private: Encapsulation in Practice
screens.narratorSegment: Encapsulation means bundling data and the methods that act on it while restricting direct access to internal details. In C# you use public and private to control visibility. Public members are accessible from outside the class; private members are only accessible inside the class. Consider health as an internal state: making health private forces external code to call TakeDamage instead of editing health directly. That method can clamp values, trigger events, or enforce rules like preventing negative health. A common mistake is making everything public for convenience; this leads to fragile code that is hard to debug because any script can change internal state arbitrarily. A safer pattern is keep fields private and provide a small set of public methods and read-only properties for needed external access. For example, private bool _isBoss with a public IsBoss method exposes information without allowing external modification. Practice by converting a public currentHealth into a private field with a public getter method and a public TakeDamage method that enforces bounds. What bugs does this prevent in multiplayer or save/load systems? Public vs Private: Encapsulation in Practice means protect internal state with private fields and expose controlled behavior via public methods to keep objects consistent.. In practical terms, why restrict access and how to expose safe operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Protect internal state with private fields and expose controlled behavior via public methods to keep objects consistent.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Public vs Private
Side-by-side
Direct access (bad)
public int health; // anyone can change this and create inconsistent states
Encapsulated (good)
private int health; public void TakeDamage(int amount) { /* clamp and react */ }
Encapsulation lets you change the internals later without breaking other systems. It makes invariants explicit and simplifies debugging.
Concrete example
EnemyStats keeps _isBoss private and exposes IsBoss method. External code can learn about boss status without being able to toggle it arbitrarily.
Check your understanding
Which members should be public on a Projectile class: damage, speed, or owner? Explain your choice and propose access controls.

screens.title: MonoBehaviour vs Custom C# Class
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between MonoBehaviour and a plain C# class is essential for clean Unity architecture. MonoBehaviour classes inherit Unity lifecycle hooks like Awake, Start, and Update and can be attached to GameObjects in the scene. They are the bridge between your data and the Unity runtime: they handle rendering, input, physics, and scene relationships. Custom C# classes do not inherit from MonoBehaviour. You create them with new and they are perfect for data models, algorithms, or game logic that doesn't need direct scene access. A recommended pattern is to store state in a custom class, and let a MonoBehaviour component manage that instance and translate runtime events into model updates. For example, EnemyController may be a MonoBehaviour attached to an enemy GameObject and hold an EnemyStats instance that stores the enemy's data. Keep heavy Unity A P I calls in MonoBehaviour and keep model classes testable and independent. A common confusion is trying to new up a MonoBehaviour; Unity manages component creation and you should use AddComponent instead when you need a scene-attached component. Ask yourself: does this code need transforms, physics callbacks, or serialization? If not, prefer a plain class.

keyIdea.title: Role separation
keyIdea.text: MonoBehaviour for scene behavior and lifecycle; custom classes for testable, reusable data models and logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › MonoBehaviour vs Class
MonoBehaviour
  • Has Awake, Start, Update lifecycle methods.
  • Can be attached to GameObjects and access transform and components.
  • Created by Unity; use AddComponent rather than new.
Example: EnemyController attaches to an enemy GameObject and uses EnemyStats instance for state.
Custom C# class
  • Created with new, no Unity lifecycle hooks.
  • Great for data models, algorithms, and logic independent of the scene.
  • Easy to unit test because it has no engine dependencies.
Key Takeaway
Separate concerns: let MonoBehaviour manage scene and engine interactions, and keep models engine-agnostic.

screens.title: PlayerStats and PlayerController — Live-Coding Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical pattern: a PlayerStats class as a pure data model and a PlayerController MonoBehaviour that creates and uses it. PlayerStats contains a public playerName and a private health field. The constructor initializes both. PlayerController's Awake or Start method calls new PlayerStats to create instances like player1 or player2 and stores them in fields or a collection. When PlayerController wants to reduce health, it calls player1. TakeDamage with an amount. Because health is private, external scripts cannot set health to invalid values directly. This pattern keeps runtime code separate from serializable behavior: PlayerController remains the scene-facing script while PlayerStats holds testable logic. A common beginner error is attempting to access private fields in another script which causes compile-time errors; use public methods or properties instead. Practice by instantiating two players with different names and health, then invoke TakeDamage on one and confirm the other is unchanged. Reflect: how does this pattern simplify saving and loading player data? keyIdea.title: Pattern summary
keyIdea.text: Use PlayerStats for state and PlayerController for runtime orchestration; instantiate models with new inside MonoBehaviour methods.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › PlayerStats Pattern
PlayerStats (non-MonoBehaviour)
// conceptual snippet
public class PlayerStats {
    public string playerName;
    private int health;
    public PlayerStats(string name, int hp) { /* set fields */ }
    public void TakeDamage(int amount) { /* reduce health safely */ }
}
PlayerController (MonoBehaviour)
Awake creates PlayerStats instances and Update triggers behavior. Controller bridges scene events to model updates and UI.
Pro tip
Keep input and presentation in the controller; put business rules like damage calculation in the model class for easier testing.

screens.title: Fields and Methods: Data vs Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Fields represent the state of an object—values like name, health, and attackPower—while methods represent actions the object can perform. In the EnemyStats example, enemyName, health, and attackPower are fields; TakeDamage and IsBoss are methods. Methods encapsulate logic that might change fields, enforce rules, and perform side effects like logging. This separation clarifies intent: data shows what the object knows; methods show what it can do. When designing, ask whether a concern is state or behavior. If it's state, it belongs as a field. screens.title: Collections of Objects: Managing Many Instances
screens.narratorSegment: Games usually have many instances of similar objects: multiple enemies, many inventory items, or a collection of quests. Use standard collections like List to store and manage these instances. For example, InventoryManager holds a List of InventoryItem objects. At Start, create items with new and add them to the list. Then iterate with foreach to display or update each item. This pattern centralizes runtime management in a MonoBehaviour while the items themselves remain lightweight data models. Be mindful of reference semantics: the List holds references to objects, so modifying an item through its reference will reflect in the list. When removing items, update the list safely to avoid enumerator invalidation. A typical mistake is storing copies or trying to serialize transient runtime-only objects as scene components. Instead, keep your model objects in memory and only serialize persistent fields when you need to save and load. Practice by adding and removing items at runtime, then logging the list contents to confirm state changes. How would you display the list in UI? Consider a simple loop that writes names and counts to text elements.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: This slide covers common errors you will encounter and how to resolve them. First, trying to access a private field from another class produces a compile-time error; the fix is to expose a public method or property that safely exposes or modifies that state. Second, attempting to instantiate a MonoBehaviour with new fails; MonoBehaviours must be created by the engine via AddComponent or by placing them on GameObjects in the scene. Third, leaving fields uninitialized and assuming defaults can produce logic bugs; prefer constructors that guarantee valid starting values. Another frequent problem is sharing mutable objects unintentionally: passing the same object reference to multiple managers can create surprising side effects. The remedy is to clone state when needed or ensure single ownership and clear documentation. When debugging, log creation and method calls inside constructors and methods to trace state changes. Finally, test small units like PlayerStats separately before integrating them into MonoBehaviour code. Which of these errors have you seen before, and how did you track them down? screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential ideas. First, a class is a blueprint: it defines fields and methods that describe what an object knows and can do. Second, an object or instance is a concrete realization of that blueprint created with new and initialized by a constructor. Third, encapsulation protects internal state using private fields and exposes safe operations with public methods and getters. Fourth, MonoBehaviour classes are special Unity components with lifecycle hooks and scene access; custom C# classes are plain models instantiated with new and are ideal for testable logic. Keep models separate from scene behavior, use constructors to ensure valid state, store multiple instances in collections like List, and avoid accessing private members externally. These practices increase modularity, reduce bugs, and make code easier to maintain and extend. Today you will learn how object-oriented design helps structure game code by separating data models from Unity components. Imagine a car template that describes color, speed, and a drive action. That template is a class. When you build a red car and a blue car from that template, those are objects, each holding their own state but sharing behaviors. In Unity you often use a lightweight data class for the model and a MonoBehaviour for the scene behavior. This separation makes systems easier to test, reuse, and reason about. As we go, you'll see concrete C# examples: a PlayerStats data class with a private health field and a public TakeDamage method, and a PlayerController MonoBehaviour that instantiates PlayerStats and calls its methods. You will also learn why constructors matter, how the new keyword creates instances, and how public and private control who can read or modify data. By the end you'll be able to design a simple Enemy or Inventory item class and connect it to a MonoBehaviour manager. Consider now: which parts of your game are pure data models and which belong on GameObjects?

By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain classes, objects, and encapsulation in your own words, define a custom C# class and its constructor, create object instances and interact with their fields and methods, and relate these custom classes to Unity MonoBehaviour components. First, you will learn to identify where data belongs: in a reusable class or attached to a scene object. Second, you will write a constructor that safely initializes an object's state and see why constructors prevent uninitialized data. Third, you will practice creating instances using the new keyword and calling public methods to change state rather than mutating private fields directly. Finally, you will map these ideas to Unity: when to use a MonoBehaviour to run scene logic and when to use a plain class as a data model. Each objective links a practical skill to why it matters in game code, and you'll complete a small hands-on activity creating inventory items and a manager to hold them. These skills reduce bugs and make your systems easier to extend.

This second objectives slide ties skills to a hands-on activity. You will create an InventoryItem class as a pure data model and then manage instances from an InventoryManager MonoBehaviour. That practice teaches how to store multiple objects in a List and iterate over them. You will see how constructors initialize each item's properties and how private fields are protected from outside mutation, while public methods allow controlled changes like using a consumable. The activity reinforces why we separate visual, scene-managed behavior from plain C# objects: many game systems need data only, not a full component lifecycle. During the activity you will attach the manager to a GameObject, run the scene, and observe console logs that show creation, state changes, and method calls. This exercise prepares you for typical patterns like enemy stats stored separately from enemy controllers, and it trains you to avoid direct field mutation which often causes bugs.

A class is a blueprint that groups related data and behavior into a single, named unit. In game development we use classes to represent players, enemies, items, or systems. A class declares fields—variables that hold data like health or name—and methods—functions that act on that data like TakeDamage or UseItem. Defining a class lets you express a concept once and reuse that definition to create many instances. For a concrete example, the EnemyStats class defines enemyName, health, attackPower, and a TakeDamage method. The constructor sets initial values when you create an enemy. It matters because when you change the behavior in one place, all instances reflect that change. A common misconception is to think classes hold runtime-only scene references; they can be pure data models with no knowledge of Unity's lifecycle. Use small, focused classes to model data and keep Unity-specific behavior in MonoBehaviour scripts. Practice by writing a class for a collectible item with fields for name, description, id, and stack size. Then add a UseItem method that decrements stack size if the item is consumable. This teaches cohesion and simplifies testing. How would you change one method to affect all items at once?

Constructors are special methods that run when you create an object. They have the same name as the class and no return value. Their job is to set fields to sensible starting values so the object is ready to use. For example, in EnemyStats the constructor accepts name, initialHealth, attackPower, and isBossEnemy and assigns them to fields. When you call new EnemyStats with those arguments, the constructor runs and logs creation. Constructors prevent mistakes like uninitialized fields and let you enforce invariants—such as ensuring current health never exceeds max health. A common mistake is exposing uninitialized public fields and then forgetting to set them before use. Another misuse is putting heavy Unity-only initialization into constructors of objects that will be serialized or created differently. In Unity, prefer constructors for pure C# classes and reserve Awake or Start for MonoBehaviour lifecycle initialization. Practice: write a PlayerStats constructor that sets playerName and health, then create two instances with different starting health. How does changing the constructor signature affect existing instantiation sites? Constructors and Initializing Objects means use constructors to create valid objects and prevent uninitialized or inconsistent state.. In practical terms, how constructors set an object's starting state and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating an object in C# uses the new keyword. That call allocates an instance, runs its constructor, and returns a reference you can store. In Unity, you often do this inside a MonoBehaviour method such as Awake or Start. For example, in GameManager or InventoryManager you might write new InventoryItem to create potions and swords and then add them to a List. After creating instances, you access public fields and call methods on them to change state. Importantly, each variable that holds the reference points to a distinct object; modifying one object does not change others. A typical flow is: define class, call new with constructor arguments, store the reference in a collection, and invoke methods like UseItem. A common misunderstanding is treating new as cloning; it always creates a fresh object. Another subtle point is reference semantics: when you pass an object reference to another variable or method, both refer to the same instance. Practice by instantiating two PlayerStats objects with different names and health, then call TakeDamage on one and observe that the other remains unchanged. Why does that separation help when building many enemies or items?

Encapsulation means bundling data and the methods that act on it while restricting direct access to internal details. In C# you use public and private to control visibility. Public members are accessible from outside the class; private members are only accessible inside the class. That method can clamp values, trigger events, or enforce rules like preventing negative health. MonoBehaviour classes inherit Unity lifecycle hooks like Awake, Start, and Update and can be attached to GameObjects in the scene. Let's summarize the essential ideas. First, a class is a blueprint: it defines fields and methods that describe what an object knows and can do. Second, an object or instance is a concrete realization of that blueprint created with new and initialized by a constructor. Third, encapsulation protects internal state using private fields and exposes safe operations with public methods and getters. Fourth, MonoBehaviour classes are special Unity components with lifecycle hooks and scene access; custom C# classes are plain models instantiated with new and are ideal for testable logic. Keep models separate from scene behavior, use constructors to ensure valid state, store multiple instances in collections like List, and avoid accessing private members externally. These practices increase modularity, reduce bugs, and make code easier to maintain and extend. As you proceed, apply these principles to enemies, players, items, and managers to build clear, reliable systems.

End with three short reminders you can apply immediately. First, design small, focused classes that represent clear responsibilities. Second, prefer private fields with public methods to preserve invariants and minimize bugs from arbitrary external changes. Third, separate data and scene logic: use plain C# classes for models and MonoBehaviour for lifecycle and scene interactions. Together these practices keep your code modular and make it easier to extend as your game's complexity grows.
